Most of her changes have come out of those mornings rather than out of the office.

title: Nine Days After the Snow Stopped
text: The snow that killed two skiers in the Thal valley in 2030 had fallen nine days earlier, and the accident is the clearest local illustration of why avalanche forecasting is difficult to communicate. Most people's model of avalanche risk is intuitive and largely correct for one kind of hazard: it snows, the new snow is unstable, the danger is high, and after a few days it settles and the danger falls. For wind slab and for storm snow this is broadly how it behaves. A persistent weak layer does not behave that way at all. Such a layer forms in particular conditions — often a period of cold, clear weather producing faceted crystals or surface hoar — and is then buried by subsequent snowfall. It can sit under the surface for weeks. It does not consolidate on the timescale the rest of the snowpack does, and it can fail long after every intuitive signal says the hazard has passed. Nine days after the last significant snowfall is exactly when such a layer is most dangerous, because that is when people have concluded the situation is safe. The slope was rated at moderate. The Vellanberg bulletin that morning described the layer, where it sat and what it would do. The investigation found the party had read the bulletin. They had taken the danger level and had not read the description beneath it. The service has covered the valley since 1981 and its forecasts were, and are, accurate; it publishes its accuracy record at the end of each winter. The failure in 2030 was not one of prediction. It was that the most important information in the bulletin was in the place readers had already stopped reading. Lena Brunner had been arguing for a change of format since 2019 and had been turned down twice. The season after the accident, the bulletin was restructured to lead with the problem type and put the danger level lower down. The second change was the audio bulletin: ninety seconds, published at six each morning, spoken by a forecaster. About 60 percent of users now listen to it rather than reading the text. The reasoning is that a listener cannot skip ahead. The order is set by the person who wrote it, and the persistent weak layer is near the beginning. Two neighbouring services have since adopted the problem-led format. What Vellanberg has refused to do is claim that any of this has saved anybody. Most accidents in the region happen at level two or three, the annual numbers are small, and Brunner has said repeatedly that four years of data cannot distinguish a better bulletin from a run of ordinary winters. The service digs about 400 snow profiles a season and has six forecasters. The slope where the two skiers died is unremarkable and is skied regularly. There is no marker on it and the service has resisted suggestions that there should be. Brunner's stated reason is that a memorial on one slope implies the others are safe, and that the whole problem the bulletin exists to address is that they are not.

title: Four Point One to Nought Point Six
text: Pellingham's contamination rate fell from 4.1 percent to 0.6 in a single year, and the change that did it was replacing plastic bags with paper ones. The plant has processed the district's food and garden waste since 2016, handling about 42,000 tonnes a year from three authorities. Finished compost is sold to farms within 30 kilometres. Contamination is measured by hand-sorting samples from every incoming load, which is tedious and is the only method that works. What was turning up, consistently, was fragments of plastic film. The puzzling part was that the district had switched to compostable bags years earlier, precisely to avoid this. Compostable plastics do break down. They do so under specified conditions — sustained temperature over a sustained period — and a windrow does not reach those conditions uniformly. The outside of a pile is cooler than the middle. A bag on the outside of a windrow for the active phase may emerge substantially intact. At that point it is screened out as contamination, which is precisely what a non-compostable bag would do. The trigger for the investigation was a farm buyer rejecting a batch in 2030. Tunde Bakare, who had taken over the plant in 2027, went back through the sampling records and found the contamination was not evenly spread. It concentrated in loads from a single collection round covering about 9,000 households in the north of the district. That round was not doing anything wrong. It was, in fact, the round with the highest participation rate, which meant it was producing the most bags, which meant it was the round where the failure of the bags showed up first. The district switched to paper liners in 2031. Paper breaks down within days regardless of where it sits in the pile, and the contamination figure went to 0.6 percent. It costs the authority about 40,000 a year more. Bakare has been straightforward about this and has argued it is cheaper than a rejected batch. The second change was the rejection policy. Pellingham now refuses any load testing above 2 percent contamination and returns it to the collecting authority. This was unpopular and is the reason the figure has stayed low. A plant that accepts contaminated material absorbs the cost of screening it, and the authority that collected it never sees a consequence. Returning the load puts the cost where the collection decision was made. Two other plants in the region have adopted the same policy. The windrows are turned every four days during the active phase, which is frequent and is part of why the plant reaches temperature as reliably as it does. Even so, the outside of a windrow never reaches the temperature of its core, and no amount of turning makes it uniform. Bakare has said this is the fact the compostable bag industry has never addressed, and that a material specified for conditions that real plants do not reliably produce is a material that will fail in the field. He has put this point to two manufacturers and reports that neither disputed the physics. What they dispute is whether the standard should describe a laboratory or a windrow, which he regards as the entire question.

title: Tunde Bakare Went Back Through the Samples
text: When a farm buyer rejected a batch of Pellingham compost in 2030, the obvious explanation was that somebody had put the wrong thing in a bin. Tunde Bakare did not accept it, mostly because the district's contamination figure had been stubbornly flat for years rather than spiking. He had managed waste operations for twelve years before taking the plant over in 2027. Pellingham processes about 42,000 tonnes a year from three authorities and sells finished compost to farms within 30 kilometres. Contamination is sampled by hand from every incoming load. That produces a great deal of data which had, until 2030, been used only to report a district-wide percentage. Bakare disaggregated it, which took a fortnight and required nothing but the records already held. What emerged was that the 4.1 percent district figure was an average concealing a very uneven distribution. Most rounds were well under 2 percent. One round, covering about 9,000 households in the north, was far higher. The instinctive conclusion was that the households on that round were careless, and Bakare has said he held that view for about a day. What changed it was the composition of the contamination. It was not tins and glass, which is what careless sorting produces. It was plastic film, almost entirely, and the district had moved to compostable bags years earlier specifically to eliminate it. The bags were the problem. Compostable plastics require sustained temperature to break down, a windrow is not uniformly hot, and a bag that spends the active phase on the cool outside of a pile survives it. The round with the highest contamination turned out to be the round with the highest participation, producing the most bags. Bakare's recommendation was paper liners, which decompose within days wherever they sit. The switch happened in 2031 and contamination fell to 0.6 percent. It costs about 40,000 a year more. His second proposal was harder to carry. Pellingham now rejects loads above 2 percent contamination and sends them back. He has defended this as an alignment of incentives rather than a punishment. A plant that quietly screens contaminated material is paying for a decision taken by somebody else, and the somebody else receives no signal at all. Returning the load means the authority that chose the collection method meets the cost of that choice. He is conscious that this is easier to say from a plant with three customers than from one with a single dependent contract, and has said he would probably not have proposed it in a weaker position. Two other regional plants have adopted it. Bakare regards the disaggregation of the sampling data as the real lesson, on the grounds that the figures had been sitting in the office the entire time. The plant now reports contamination by round rather than by district, which takes an extra hour a month and which he describes as the cheapest process improvement of his career. Two other plants in the region have adopted the practice, and one found a comparable problem within a season. Its cause was different — a single commercial customer rather than a collection round — and it was found the same way, by disaggregating a figure that had been reported as an average for years.

title: The Bags Were Supposed to Fix It
text: The district moved to compostable plastic bags in order to solve a contamination problem. The bags became the contamination problem, and it took about seven years to notice. Pellingham has composted the district's food and garden waste since 2016, handling around 42,000 tonnes a year from three authorities. The compost goes to farms within 30 kilometres, which means the buyers inspect it and will refuse it. The original problem was ordinary plastic film — carrier bags used as bin liners, which do not break down and which have to be screened out. Compostable bags were the industry answer and the district adopted them. They are not a fraud. Compostable plastics do decompose, under the right conditions, and those conditions are specified: sustained temperature over sustained time. A windrow does not provide them uniformly. The middle of a pile runs hot; the outside does not. Material spends the active phase wherever it happens to be, and a bag on the cool outside can come through the process essentially unchanged. At that point it is indistinguishable, to a screen and to a farm buyer, from a conventional carrier bag. The district's contamination rate sat around 4.1 percent for years. This was regarded as a background level and was reported as a district figure, which is what concealed the cause. In 2030 a farm buyer rejected a batch. Tunde Bakare, manager since 2027, broke the sampling records down by collection round and found the contamination concentrated in one round of about 9,000 households. The resolution was counterintuitive. That round had the district's highest participation rate. More households composting meant more bags, and more bags meant more of them surviving the process. The households doing it best were producing the worst material. Paper liners were adopted in 2031. They break down within days wherever they sit in a pile, and contamination fell to 0.6 percent. The paper costs the authority about 40,000 a year more than the plastic did. Pellingham also began rejecting loads over 2 percent and returning them, which two other regional plants have since copied. What the episode is now cited for has less to do with composting than with measurement. The district had seven years of sampling data that contained the answer. It was collected properly, filed properly, and reported as a single average, and an average across an uneven population is an excellent way of hiding a localised cause. Nothing new was measured in 2030. The records were simply sorted differently, by a man who had a fortnight and a reason to look. The farm buyer who rejected the batch in 2030 still takes compost from Pellingham and is, by general agreement in the district, the person most responsible for the improvement. Nobody has ever thanked them publicly, which Bakare has said he intends to correct and has not yet got round to. The relationship with that buyer is, if anything, better than before. They still sample every delivery and the plant regards this as entirely reasonable, on the view that a customer who checks is a customer who will notice a problem before it becomes a rejected year.

title: Quota That Cannot Leave
text: The Haldvik association owns its quota collectively and no member can sell any of it. A boat that does not use its allocation returns it to the pool, and it is reallocated the following year. This is the rule the whole arrangement rests on, and it exists because of what happened before it. Haldvik has about 1,300 residents and the fishery is its largest employer. In 2000 the district had 61 boats. By 2013 it had 22. The mechanism was not overfishing. It was sale. Under the previous system quota was held individually and could be sold to any buyer anywhere, and a skipper approaching retirement with a quota holding worth a substantial sum had every reason to sell it and no reason to sell it locally. Each sale was entirely rational for the person making it. The aggregate effect was that the district's fishing rights left, boat by boat, over about thirteen years, and the processing jobs followed them. The association took the quota into collective ownership in 2014. Members receive an annual allocation, and the allocation is a right to fish rather than an asset they own. A member leaving the fishery therefore takes nothing with them. What they had reverts to the pool. This was challenged in 2022 by a member who wished to sell, and was upheld. The allocation rules have two further features that matter. Unused quota returns to the pool at the end of the year, which removes any advantage in holding an allocation you do not intend to fish. And a new entrant receives a starter allocation for three years at no cost. That last provision is the reason there have been new entrants at all. Under the previous arrangement a person wanting to start fishing at Haldvik had to buy quota at market value, which was prohibitive for anybody who had not inherited it. Three new entrants have joined since 2019 and boat numbers have been stable at 24. The second rule concerns landings. Members must sell through the Haldvik market, which employs 34 people in processing and handling. This is more contentious than the quota rule, because a skipper can sometimes get a better price elsewhere on a given day. The association's position is that a fishery which lands its catch in another district has exported its processing jobs and will eventually export the boats as well. Two members were expelled in 2026 for landing outside the district. The association publishes every boat's allocation and landings annually, which makes the rules enforceable by the membership rather than only by the chair. Average boat age has fallen from 31 years to 19 since 2014, which is the figure Dahl cites most often. A fleet with an average boat age of 31 is a fleet nobody is investing in. Skippers do not replace a boat they expect to sell out of, and the fall to 19 years is the clearest evidence the association has that its members now regard themselves as having a future in the fishery rather than an asset to realise.

title: Sigrid Dahl Made the Quota Worthless to Sell
text: Sigrid Dahl skippered out of Haldvik for nineteen years and watched the fleet fall from 61 boats to 22, largely by the voluntary decisions of people she knew. She took the association chair in 2016, two years after the quota had been brought into collective ownership, and her contribution has been the set of rules that stopped the collective holding from leaking away the same way the individual ones had. The original problem is easy to describe and was extremely hard to stop. Quota held individually is an asset. A skipper who has fished for forty years and is coming to the end of it holds something valuable, and selling it is the most sensible thing a person in that position can do. Nobody in Haldvik behaved badly. Between 2000 and 2013 the district's fishing rights were sold, boat by boat, to buyers elsewhere, by people making defensible decisions about their own retirement. Collective ownership in 2014 addressed the stock holding. What Dahl saw was that it did not by itself address the incentive. Her rule is that unused quota returns to the pool. A member who stops fishing takes nothing. A member who holds an allocation and does not use it loses it at the end of the year. The effect is to make the allocation worthless as an asset and valuable only as a right to fish. Nobody has anything to sell, so nobody is in the position that emptied the district before. This was tested legally in 2022 by a member who wanted to realise value and was upheld. Her second rule was the starter allocation: three years, free, for a new entrant. Dahl has been blunt about why. Under the old system, entering the fishery meant buying quota at market price, which meant that fishing at Haldvik was available to people who inherited it and to nobody else. Three new entrants have come in since 2019. Boat numbers have held at 24 and average boat age has fallen from 31 to 19. The landing requirement is the rule she has had most trouble with. Members must sell through the Haldvik market, which employs 34 people, and a skipper can occasionally do better elsewhere. Two members were expelled in 2026. Dahl has declined to discuss the individuals and has been unambiguous about the principle: a fleet that lands elsewhere loses its market, and a fleet without a market loses its boats within a decade. She publishes every allocation and every landing figure annually. Her stated reason is that a rule enforced by one person is a rule that ends when that person does, and she is conscious of being sixty-three. The association has begun training two younger members in how the allocation is calculated, which she regards as the most important thing she is currently doing and the one that will be judged long after she has stopped. She has said the rules are simple enough to survive her and that the understanding of why they exist may not be. Nobody under forty in Haldvik remembers the fleet at 61 boats, and to a younger member the rules can look like an arbitrary restriction on an asset they are told they do not own. Dahl spends a good deal of her time explaining the years from 2000 to 2013 to people who were children during them.

title: Sixty-One Boats
text: Haldvik had 61 boats in 2000. By 2013 it had 22, and nothing had happened to the fish. This is the part outsiders find hardest to follow. There was no stock collapse, no closure, no disaster. The fishery was in reasonable condition throughout. What left was the right to fish it. Quota in that period was held individually and could be sold to any buyer anywhere. For a skipper at the end of a career it represented the accumulated value of a working life, and selling it was how that value was realised. Each transaction was between consenting parties and was nobody else's business. The cumulative effect over thirteen years was that Haldvik, a place of about 1,300 people whose largest employer was the fishery, lost roughly two thirds of its fleet. The processing jobs went with the boats, because a market with nothing landing into it does not survive. The association took the remaining quota into collective ownership in 2014. Members now receive an annual allocation which is a right to fish rather than a possession, and unused allocation returns to the pool. The critical feature is that there is nothing left to sell. A member leaving takes nothing with them. That was challenged in court in 2022 by a member who wanted to realise value from an allocation, and the association's rule was upheld. Boat numbers have been stable at 24 since 2019. Three new entrants have joined, which under the previous system would have been impossible, since entering meant buying quota at market price. The association gives a new entrant a starter allocation free for three years. Average boat age has fallen from 31 years to 19, which is the clearest sign that people are investing again. The Haldvik market employs 34 people, and members are required to land through it. Two were expelled in 2026 for landing elsewhere. What the district is careful about is that none of this recovered what was lost. Twenty-four boats is not 61. The quota sold between 2000 and 2013 is held elsewhere and is not coming back, and the association's rules govern only what remained after the bleeding stopped. Sigrid Dahl, who has chaired the association since 2016 and skippered for nineteen years before that, has put it as stabilising a decline rather than reversing one. The figures are published annually, every boat's allocation and every boat's landings, which is how the membership checks that the rules are being applied. Haldvik regards that transparency as the thing most likely to keep the arrangement alive after the people who built it have gone. The district is also conscious that its arrangement depends on the wider regulatory framework continuing to permit it. Collective holding of quota is not the standard model, the 2022 challenge established only that the association's own rules bind its own members, and a change in national policy could unpick the whole thing without anybody in Haldvik being consulted. The association has therefore spent money on legal advice it would rather have spent elsewhere, and keeps a watching brief on policy consultations. Dahl has described this as the least visible and most necessary work the association does.

title: Worst First
text: The Thorne Vale archive digitises its worst film first. Everything else about the operation follows from that decision, and it was not the original plan. The archive holds 41,000 reels of regional newsreel and amateur footage covering 1921 to 1994, in a former cold store, with seven staff. About 11,000 reels had been scanned by 2034. The plan Ravi Chandrasekar inherited in 2026 worked chronologically from 1921 forwards. This is the intuitive approach and it has real advantages: it produces a coherent run, it is easy to explain to funders, and it means the oldest material is done soonest. It is also, for this collection, close to the worst possible order. About 3,000 of the reels are cellulose nitrate. Nitrate is flammable, which is the property everybody knows, and it decays autocatalytically, which is the property that matters more. The products of decomposition catalyse further decomposition, so a reel that has started to go will go faster as it proceeds. A chronological programme scans material in the order it was made. It has no relationship to the order in which material is dying. Chandrasekar reversed it. The archive now assesses condition and scans the most degraded stock first, regardless of date, subject or how interesting anybody finds it. The consequence is a digital collection that looks incoherent — fragments from across seven decades, with no runs and no narrative — and which contains the material that would otherwise have been lost. Roughly 600 reels were found to be beyond scanning when they were assessed. Those are gone and the archive says so in its catalogue. Nitrate is stored separately, in a bunker at 4 degrees, in individual cells so that a fire in one does not propagate. Scanning takes between 40 minutes and four hours a reel depending on condition. The archive refuses requests to digitise out of order, including from broadcasters, and this is the policy that generates the most friction. A production company wanting a particular 1950s reel for a programme with a transmission date is offered a place in the condition-based queue and nothing else. Chandrasekar has held this without exception since 2026. The reels are kept after scanning rather than disposed of. This costs storage and is disputed within the profession, on the reasonable argument that a 4K scan is better than a decaying original and the original is a fire risk. The archive's position is that scanning standards keep improving and that a disposed reel cannot be rescanned. Everything digitised goes out under an open licence and has been used in about 400 productions. The most requested item is a 1937 reel of a flood at Thorne Vale. That reel is four minutes long, was shot by somebody the archive cannot name, and has been used more than any professionally made footage in the collection. Chandrasekar offers it as the argument against trying to predict what will matter, which is the other reason the archive scans by condition rather than by interest. Nobody in 1937 thought the footage was important; it was a man with a camera and a flooded street. What made it valuable was the flood of 2031, which nobody could have predicted and which no acquisition policy could have planned around.

title: Ravi Chandrasekar Reversed the Queue
text: Ravi Chandrasekar's first act at Thorne Vale was to stop the digitisation programme, which had been running successfully for three years and was ahead of schedule. He had worked in film restoration for fifteen years before taking the post in 2026. The archive holds 41,000 reels from 1921 to 1994 in a converted cold store and employs seven people. The programme he stopped was working chronologically from 1921. It was competent, it was producing good scans, and it had the support of everybody involved. His objection was that it had been designed around the collection rather than around the film. A chronological scan treats the archive as a historical sequence to be worked through. That is what an archive is for cataloguing purposes. Physically, it is 41,000 objects in varying states of decay, about 3,000 of them cellulose nitrate, which decays autocatalytically and therefore accelerates as it goes. Nothing about the date a film was shot tells you how close it is to being unrecoverable. Chandrasekar reordered the whole programme around condition assessment. The archive now scans the worst material first, whatever it is and whenever it was made. He has been candid about the cost. The digital collection is a mess. It has no runs, no chronological coherence, and it frustrates researchers who want a decade rather than a scattering of reels across seventy years. His answer is that coherence can be assembled later from a complete digital collection, and cannot be assembled at all from film that has gone. The assessment itself produced the worst news of his tenure. Roughly 600 reels were found to be beyond scanning. He publishes those in the catalogue with a note saying what they were, which he has described as the least he can do and the most he can do. His hardest position to hold has been the refusal to digitise on request. Broadcasters approach the archive wanting a specific reel for a specific programme, often with money attached, and Chandrasekar offers them the condition queue. He has conceded that this loses the archive income and has argued it is the only defensible rule. Once the queue can be bought, the order is set by whoever is making a programme this year, and the material nobody happens to want in 2034 is the material that will be gone by 2044. The reels are kept after scanning, which is contested in the profession. His reasoning is that scanning technology has improved continuously throughout his career and that a disposed original forecloses every future improvement. Everything scanned goes out under an open licence. About 400 productions have used it, which he regards as the justification for the whole enterprise and as entirely separate from the question of what order to work in. He is asked regularly whether the open licence costs the archive income it needs. His answer is that the material was made in this district, largely by amateurs, and that charging a local historian to look at a film of their own street is a position he is not prepared to defend. The archive does charge for commissioned scanning work, which it undertakes for other institutions and which brings in a modest income. That work is done outside the condition queue, on other people's material, and does not displace anything at Thorne Vale.

title: The Flood Reel of 1937
text: The most requested item at Thorne Vale is four minutes of a flood in 1937, shot by somebody whose name the archive does not know. It is the archive's most-used footage by a wide margin, has appeared in dozens of productions, and is the thing local people ask for when they come in. It was digitised in 2029 because it was in poor condition, not because anybody had requested it. Under the archive's previous programme, which worked chronologically from 1921, it would have been reached around 2031. Whether it would still have been scannable is the question nobody can answer. The archive holds 41,000 reels covering 1921 to 1994, in a former cold store, with seven staff. About 11,000 had been digitised by 2034. Roughly 3,000 reels are cellulose nitrate, which is both flammable and subject to autocatalytic decay: the products of decomposition catalyse further decomposition, so deterioration speeds up once it starts. Nitrate is held in a separate bunker at 4 degrees in individual cells. Ravi Chandrasekar, archivist since 2026, reversed the digitisation order so that the most degraded material is scanned first regardless of date or subject. The consequence is a digital collection without shape. There are no complete runs. A researcher wanting the 1950s finds fragments rather than a decade. What there is, instead, is the material that was about to disappear. About 600 reels were assessed as beyond scanning. The archive lists them in its catalogue, with whatever is known about what they contained, which is a melancholy document and was a deliberate decision. The 1937 flood reel is the counterexample that justifies the policy locally. It is not important footage by any national measure; it is four minutes of water in a street in a small place. Thorne Vale flooded again in 2031, and the 1937 film was used extensively in the argument about what should be built afterwards. People could see where the water had gone before, in the same streets, under the same bridge. That use was not anticipated by anybody and could not have been. The reel was scanned because it was decaying, by a programme that does not consider what footage is for. Everything the archive digitises is published under an open licence and has been used in about 400 productions. The physical reels are retained after scanning, which costs storage and is disputed by people who point out that a 4K scan is better than a decaying original and that nitrate is a fire risk. Thorne Vale's answer is that scanning standards have improved throughout the lifetime of every archivist now working, and that a reel which has been destroyed cannot benefit from whatever comes next. The archive has never disposed of anything and does not intend to, which it acknowledges is easier to say in a building that was designed to keep things cold. The cold store helps the argument considerably. The building the archive occupies was designed to hold things at low temperature and does so cheaply, which means retaining 41,000 reels after scanning is a marginal cost rather than a prohibitive one. Chandrasekar has conceded that an archive in an ordinary warehouse might reasonably reach a different conclusion.

title: Seven People and Forty-One Thousand Reels
text: The arithmetic at Thorne Vale is unforgiving and the staff quote it readily. Forty-one thousand reels. Seven people. Between 40 minutes and four hours to scan one, depending on what condition it is in. About 11,000 reels had been done by 2034. The programme has been running since 2023. Nobody at the archive pretends the whole collection will be digitised. The working assumption, which Ravi Chandrasekar states without any visible distress, is that a substantial proportion of it will decay beyond recovery before anybody reaches it. That assumption is why the order matters so much, and why the archive reorganised its programme around condition in 2026 rather than working chronologically from 1921. The building is a former cold store, which is the reason the archive exists in the form it does. A collection of this size needs cool, stable, dry storage, and a redundant cold store is the cheapest way any small organisation is going to get it. Nitrate — about 3,000 reels of it — is held separately, in a bunker at 4 degrees, in individual cells. The cells are there so that a fire in one reel does not take the rest. Staff are matter-of-fact about the fire risk in a way that visitors find unsettling. Nitrate burns readily, produces its own oxygen, and cannot be extinguished by conventional means. The archive's approach is containment rather than prevention. The scanning itself is 4K and slow. A reel in good condition runs through in under an hour. A reel that has begun to shrink has to be handled frame by frame in places, and four hours is not unusual. Condition assessment happens first, and it is what sets the queue. About 600 reels have been assessed as beyond scanning and are catalogued as such. The archive will not scan to order. Broadcasters have offered money for specific reels and have been refused, on the grounds that a purchasable queue is a queue ordered by whoever is making programmes this year. Everything scanned is published under an open licence. Around 400 productions have used the material, and the archive charges nothing for any of it. Asked whether an open licence is affordable for an organisation of seven people with 30,000 reels still to do, the answer given is that the licence costs nothing to grant and that a charged archive is used by fewer people, which weakens the case for funding it. The reels are kept after scanning. Storage costs money the archive does not obviously have, and the justification offered is consistent with everything else here: scanning will improve, the originals are the only route to that improvement, and a decision to destroy is the one decision that cannot be revisited. The profession is not united on this and the archive does not pretend that it is. Staff describe the work as repetitive and say the compensation is that nobody knows what is on a reel until it runs. A can labelled as a council opening in 1954 turned out to contain fifteen minutes of a street market, which is now among the collection's more used footage and appears in the catalogue under a description somebody wrote in 2033. The original label has been kept alongside the corrected one. Chandrasekar's rule is that the archive records what it was told as well as what it found, since the discrepancy is occasionally the interesting part.
